claims.text: Ab initio molecular dynamics using density functional theory can accurately predict high-temperature oxidation behavior in metallic or ceramic materials.
Ab initio molecular dynamics using density functional theory can accurately predict phase stability in metallic or ceramic materials.
The modeled initial material is crystalline and has known lattice parameters.
The material is heated above 1000 K in an oxidizing environment.
The simulation is conducted at constant pressure and temperature with an oxygen partial pressure of 1 atm.
High-temperature exposure in the oxidizing environment produces oxide-layer formation and growth.
Oxygen ions undergo thermally activated diffusion through the oxide layer.
Electrons undergo thermally activated transport through the oxide layer.
Transport of oxygen ions and electrons through the oxide layer causes oxide-layer growth.
After 10 hours of high-temperature oxidation, oxide-layer thickness will increase by 20% relative to the room-temperature baseline.
The relevant temperature range is 1000–1500 K.
The relevant oxygen partial-pressure range is 0.1–1 atm.
Prediction accuracy depends on the selected exchange-correlation functional.
Prediction accuracy depends on the quality of the pseudopotentials.
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy can be used to measure oxide-layer thickness after high-temperature oxidation.
Transmission electron microscopy can be used to measure oxide-layer thickness after high-temperature oxidation.
A measured oxide-layer thickness below 10% of the predicted value is defined as falsifying the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The intervention specifies temperatures above 1000 K, whereas the stated boundary includes exactly 1000 K.
